extracted.intended_audience: serious readers and students of philosophy (those familiar with Kant; ideally acquainted with Plato and the Upanishads)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and prerequisites for reading and translating Arthur Schopenhauer's The World as Will and Idea (Vol. I). Advises on reading order, background knowledge required, and translatoral choices to understand the work as intended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read the book twice
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The work is an organic whole whose parts presuppose one another; the first perusal demands patience and voluntary confidence that the beginning presupposes the end and vice versa. A second perusal will cast much or all in an entirely different light.

rubrics_metrics.name: First perusal demands patience
rubrics_metrics.description: The first perusal demands patience, founded on confidence that the beginning presupposes the end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect the first reading to be difficult; avoid premature disapproval rooted in misunderstandings that will often be resolved on a second reading. Do not expect every relation to be explicated at first encounter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read the introduction 'On the Fourfold Root' first
rubrics_metrics.description: The introduction (On the fourfold root of the principle of sufficient reason) must be read before the book itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Without acquaintance with this introduction the present work is 'absolutely impossible to understand properly' — its content is presupposed throughout Book I and is treated as propadeutic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know 'On Sight and Colour' for parts omitted
rubrics_metrics.description: Knowledge of the short earlier work 'On Sight and Colour' is presupposed for material omitted from Book I.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schopenhauer omitted material contained in that essay which would otherwise have appeared word for word; readers should consult it to supply those gaps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thorough acquaintance with Kant required
rubrics_metrics.description: An acquaintance with the principal writings of Kant is directly presupposed; Kant's doctrine produces a fundamental intellectual change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only those who have properly mastered Kant will be able to follow the method here attempted; reading secondary expositions is warned against — learn Kant from his own works, not second-hand accounts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read the Kant-critique appendix (recommended first)
rubrics_metrics.description: The polemic/criticism of Kant has been relegated to a special appendix and its knowledge is presupposed; it is advisable to read the appendix first.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The appendix corrects and supplements the exposition and is specially related to Book I; reading it early will aid comprehension of references in the main text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer primary sources over second-hand expositions
rubrics_metrics.description: One cannot reliably learn Kant (or other great philosophers) from expositions by others; read the original works.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recent or popular second-hand accounts (e.g., Hegelian expositions) may distort Kantian thought; extraordinary minds must be read in their own words to preserve meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read volumes in advised sequence: first volume alone, second after
rubrics_metrics.description: Read the first volume without the supplementary books on a first pass; use the supplementary (second) volume on a later perusal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The first volume explains the system; the second is a fuller elaboration and should be read after comprehension of the first to avoid excessive difficulty. Numbered references connect the two.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guard against losing sight of the principal thought
rubrics_metrics.description: In each of the four books guard against losing sight of the principal thought to which details belong.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The system is an organic unity composed of four principal divisions (aspects); when reading particulars, continually refer them back to the central idea to preserve coherence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reader suitability: not for casual or entertainment-seeking readers
rubrics_metrics.description: The book is not meant for casual readers seeking entertainment or quick gratification; it demands serious effort and specific preparation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a reader is unwilling to comply with the presupposed demands (reading background, patience, multiple readings), the author advises laying down the book rather than trying to extract superficial value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best prepared if acquainted with Plato and the Upanishads
rubrics_metrics.description: Familiarity with Plato and, especially, the Upanishads (Vedic literature) makes one better prepared to receive the work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schopenhauer states that each aphorism of the Upanishads can be deduced from his thought; such background eases reception though it is not strictly necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translator's fidelity: prefer ipsissima verba where necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a choice had to be made in translation, the alternative of 'somewhat slavish adherence to Schopenhauer's ipsissima verba' was preferred to inaccuracy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The translators note that extensive alteration of long involved sentences risks obliterating the original form and imperiling meaning; they therefore sacrifice English smoothness for fidelity in many places.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translation of key technical terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific renderings of German technical terms: 'Vorstellung' → 'idea'; 'Idee' → 'Idea' (capitalized); 'Anschauung' → 'perception' or 'intuition or perception' depending on context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The translators chose 'idea' over 'representation' for 'Vorstellung' as being more accurate, intelligible, and elegant; they explain these choices to help readers follow the philosophical terminology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translation trade-off: preserve meaning over smoothing style
rubrics_metrics.description: Extensive alteration of long and involved sentences, though potentially improving English style, tended to obliterate the form of the original or imperil the meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Therefore the translators accept stylistic faults to 'reproduce faithfully the spirit as well as the letter' of Schopenhauer; expect occasional looser or involved English style as deliberate fidelity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid reliance on contemporary academic fashions or professional aims
rubrics_metrics.description: The book presupposes that many contemporary philosophical writings serve material or professional ends; the reader should approach with the aim of pursuing truth for its own sake.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schopenhauer warns that much modern philosophical writing is driven by personal, political, or professional motives and may therefore be untrustworthy as a guide to truth; treat such works with skepticism.
